title: The Data Structures Behind Databases
summary: You will understand append-only logs, hash indexes, LSM trees and B-trees, and be able to explain the write/read/space amplification trade-offs between them.

questions.prompt: Why is appending to a log file so fast, and why is reading a key from a plain append-only log so slow?
questions.hint: Think about where on disk the write lands, and what `get` has to look at.
keyPoints: Appends are sequential I/O at the end of the file, the fastest disk access pattern; no searching or in-place rewriting.
Updates are just newer appends; the last value for a key wins.
Without an index, a read must scan the whole file: O(n) in the file size.
The fix is an index (e.g. an in-memory hash map from key to byte offset).

questions.prompt: A table has **1 billion rows**. Each B-tree leaf page holds **50 rows** and each internal page has a branching factor of **300**. How many levels does the tree need? If the root and the next level are cached in RAM and an SSD read takes **100 µs**, roughly how long does a point lookup spend on disk?
questions.hint: First count the leaf pages. Then find the smallest number of internal levels whose fan-out reaches that many leaves.
keyPoints: 300^2 = 90,000 is too few, 300^3 = 27,000,000 ≥ 20,000,000, so 3 internal levels above the leaves.
Total depth = 4 levels (root, 2 internal, leaf).
With the top 2 levels cached, about 2 disk reads ≈ 2 × 100 µs = 200 µs.
Contrast: a binary tree would need about log2(1e9) ≈ 30 levels.
questions.answer:
```text
leaves = 1e9 / 50 = 2e7
300^1 = 300
300^2 = 90,000
300^3 = 27,000,000 >= 20,000,000  -> 3 levels of internal pages
depth = 3 + 1 (leaf) = 4
disk reads = 4 - 2 cached = 2 -> ~200 µs
```

questions.prompt: Explain the write path and the read path of an **LSM tree**. Where do the memtable, SSTables, compaction and Bloom filters fit?
questions.hint: Follow one `put` from memory to disk, then follow one `get` for a key that does not exist.
keyPoints: Write: append to a write-ahead log for durability, then insert into the memtable, an in-memory sorted structure.
When the memtable is full (e.g. ~64 MB) it is flushed sequentially as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable.
Compaction merges SSTables in the background, keeping the newest value per key and dropping overwritten values and tombstones.
Read: check memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest until the key is found.
Each SSTable has a Bloom filter so a lookup can skip files that definitely do not contain the key, which matters most for missing keys.

questions.hint: Try `set("café", "☕")`. Is the offset counted in characters or in bytes?
keyPoints: `line.length` counts UTF-16 code units, but the file offsets are in bytes.
Non-ASCII text (e.g. "é", emoji) takes several UTF-8 bytes, so later offsets drift and point to the middle of other lines.
Fix: `offset += Buffer.byteLength(line)` (or `Buffer.from(line).length`).
Bonus: `get` reads the whole file; a real store would read only from the offset (e.g. `fs.readSync` with a position).
questions.answer: Replace `offset += line.length;` with `offset += Buffer.byteLength(line, 'utf8');`. `"☕".length` is 1 but it is 3 bytes in UTF-8, so every offset after a non-ASCII write is wrong (remember Day 3).

questions.prompt: Your team must store **400,000 writes/second** of IoT sensor readings, mostly read back later as "last hour for device X". A teammate suggests PostgreSQL with a B-tree index; another suggests Cassandra (LSM-based). Compare them in terms of the storage engine.
questions.hint: Which structure turns random writes into sequential writes?
keyPoints: B-tree updates pages in place: random writes, page splits and WAL, so very high write rates stress it.
LSM buffers writes in a memtable and flushes sequentially, so it sustains much higher write throughput.
Data sorted by (device, time) makes "last hour for device X" a range scan, which both can do; LSM reads may touch several SSTables.
Mentions amplification: LSM has compaction write amplification and space amplification; B-tree has page-rewrite write amplification.
A reasonable conclusion favors the LSM/wide-column store for this write-heavy append workload, while noting to benchmark.

questions.prompt: An app updates **20,000 rows/second**, each change is **100 bytes**. On a B-tree with **8 KB pages**, assume the worst case: every update dirties a different page that gets written out, plus the 100-byte change goes to the WAL. On an LSM engine, assume total write amplification of **15×**. Compute bytes/second hitting the disk for each and the write amplification factor of the B-tree case.
questions.hint: Write amplification = bytes written to disk / bytes the application changed.
keyPoints: App writes 20,000 × 100 B = 2 MB/s of logical data.
B-tree worst case per update: 8,192 + 100 = 8,292 B → 20,000 × 8,292 ≈ 166 MB/s.
B-tree write amplification ≈ 8,292 / 100 ≈ 83×.
LSM: 2 MB/s × 15 = 30 MB/s.
Notes real B-trees batch many updates into the same dirty page before flushing, so the average is much lower than the worst case.
